H1.text: A gas flame heats a pan. A bulb lights the room. A pressure cooker whistles.

H2.text: Heat, light and sound. Three different forms of energy. Where do they come from?

H3.text: Diya is cooking dinner. The gas burns, the pan gets hot, and the cooker whistles.

H4.text: Then the stove goes off, and the warmth fades. Was the energy used up, or did it go somewhere?

H5.text: By the end, you will know the one rule that energy never breaks.

P1.text: So what are the forms of energy?

P2.text: Energy is the ability to do work. It comes in many forms.

P3.text: Moving things have kinetic energy. Raised or stretched things store potential energy.

P4.text: Hot things have heat energy. Fuel and food store chemical energy.

P5.text: There is also electrical energy, light, sound, and nuclear energy.

P6.text: And energy keeps changing from one form to another. Chemical energy in the gas becomes heat, light and sound.

S1.text: A two kilogram block sits on a rough ramp, five metres high.

S2.text: At the top, it stores ninety eight joules of potential energy, m g h.

S3.text: Let it go. As it slides, the potential energy falls, and the kinetic energy grows.

S4.text: But friction rubs the block against the ramp. Some energy turns into heat.

S5.text: At the bottom, fifty eight joules of kinetic energy, and forty joules of heat.

S6.text: On the graph, three lines change. But the total stays flat, at ninety eight joules.

S8.text: Friction pushes back on the block, and warms both surfaces. Not a single joule disappears.

D1.text: Now let's write the rule, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. Friction does work, f times d. Four newtons times ten metres. Forty joules.

D3.text: Step two. That work does not vanish. It becomes heat, in the block and the ramp.

D4.text: Step three. So U at the top equals K at the bottom, plus the heat. Ninety eight equals fifty eight plus forty.

D5.text: Step four. The total energy of an isolated system stays constant. It changes form, but is never created or destroyed.

T1.text: Remember this. Energy is never made or lost. It only changes form.

C2.text: Mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential. With friction, it goes down. Here, from ninety eight to fifty eight joules.

C3.text: Total energy also counts heat, sound and light. That never goes down. Still ninety eight.

C4.text: Now you try. A ball bounces lower and lower, then stops. Is energy lost from the universe? Pause and decide.

C5.text: No! It became heat and sound, in the ball, the floor and the air. The total is the same.

K1.text: One more. A ceiling fan takes in electrical energy. Is all of it turned into the motion of air? Pause and think.

K2.text: No! Some becomes heat in the motor, and some the fan's hum. All of it adds up to the input.

R1.text: So where does the energy in Diya's kitchen go? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. The gas stores chemical energy. Burning turns it into heat and light.

R3.text: Two. The heat flows into the pan and the food. Some escapes into the air.

R4.text: Three. Steam in the cooker lifts the whistle. Heat becomes motion and sound.

R5.text: Four. In the end, it all spreads out as a little warmth in the room. Nothing is destroyed.

W2.text: A half kilogram ball falls from ten metres. Air drag slows it, and it lands at twelve metres per second. How much energy went into the air?

W3.text: At the top, U equals m g h. Half, times nine point eight, times ten. Forty nine joules.

W4.text: At the ground, K equals half m v squared. Half, times half, times one forty four. Thirty six joules.

W5.text: Total energy is conserved. So the air got forty nine minus thirty six. Thirteen joules, as heat.

X2.text: Many students say, energy is conserved, so the kinetic energy at the bottom must equal m g h.

X3.text: But only the total is conserved. With friction, K plus the heat equals m g h. K alone is less.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In board questions on energy changes, and in numericals where friction makes heat.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A one kilogram block slides from rest down a rough curve, five metres high, reaching the bottom at eight metres per second. It then stops in four metres on a rough floor. g is ten. Find the heat made on the curve, and the friction on the floor. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Eighteen joules, and eight newtons.

A2.text: At the top, U is m g h. One times ten times five. Fifty joules.

A3.text: At the bottom, K is half, times one, times sixty four. Thirty two joules. So the curve made eighteen joules of heat.

A4.text: On the floor, friction turns all thirty two joules into heat, in four metres. f is thirty two over four. Eight newtons.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Name four forms of energy in a kitchen.

Y3.text: Two. Where does mechanical energy go when friction acts?

Y4.text: Three. What does the law of conservation of energy say?
